blocks.text: KING OVER JUDAEA, UNDER ROME · NEW TESTAMENT
Herod Agrippa I. The king who killed James and imprisoned Peter.
RULEDi

SEAT
Not stated

“Herod the king stretched forth his hands to vex certain of the church. And he killed James the brother of…”

ROME: 17 RULERS HEROD THE GREAT → PORCIUS FESTUS
THE HERODS
Which Herod this is
SUCCESSION
Before and after
WHAT SCRIPTURE SAYS
What Scripture says of him
"Herod the king stretched forth his hands to vex certain of the church. And he killed James the brother of John with the sword." Acts 12:1–2

"Because he saw it pleased the Jews, he proceeded further to take Peter also", in "the days of unleavened bread". He set four quaternions of soldiers to guard him, "intending after Easter to bring him forth to the people". Acts 12:3–4
From the textThe KJV's "Easter" in Acts 12:4 translates the same Greek word it renders "Passover" in Luke 22:1. Acts 12:4 Luke 22:1

The church prayed without ceasing. On the night before Herod would have brought him out, an angel freed Peter, who said, "the Lord hath sent his angel, and hath delivered me out of the hand of Herod". Acts 12:5–11
"When Herod had sought for him, and found him not, he examined the keepers, and commanded that they should be put to death." Then he went down from Judaea to Caesarea. Acts 12:18–19
He "was highly displeased with them of Tyre and Sidon"; through Blastus, "the king's chamberlain", they asked for peace, "because their country was nourished by the king's country". Acts 12:20

"Upon a set day Herod, arrayed in royal apparel, sat upon his throne, and made an oration". The people shouted, "It is the voice of a god, and not of a man." "And immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory: and he was eaten of worms, and gave up the ghost." Acts 12:21–23
"But the word of God grew and multiplied." Acts 12:24

SCRIPTURE'S NUMBERS
No years given
None. Acts sets his persecution "about that time", after the famine foretold for "the days of Claudius Caesar" (Acts 11:28; 12:1).
SCHÜRER (1890)
King of Philip's former tetrarchy from AD 37, of Antipas's from about AD 40, of Judaea and Samaria from AD 41; died at Caesarea in AD 44.
6 August 44, at the regular games founded by Herod
Wieseler, followed by A. C. McGiffert (1890)
McGiffert thinks the festival was more probably the five-yearly games Herod the Great instituted for Augustus, and gives Wieseler's date of 6 August 44.[2]

WHAT SCRIPTURE DOES NOT SAY
Acts never calls him Agrippa, and does not say whose son or grandson he was.
Acts does not say why he was displeased with Tyre and Sidon.
Acts gives no year for his death.
IDENTIFICATIONS THIS PAGE RELIES ON

From the textActs calls him only "Herod the king". He acts in Judaea, goes down "from Judaea to Caesarea", and dies there. Acts never calls him Agrippa and does not say whose son he was. Acts 12:1 Acts 12:19–23
Early church · Eusebius, tr. A. C. McGiffert, 1890Eusebius (about AD 325) heads his chapter on Acts 12 "Agrippa, who was also called Herod" (Church History 2.10).[19]
From the textHe is not the "Herod the tetrarch" of Acts 13:1, the verse after his story ends; that is Herod Antipas. Acts 12:23 Acts 13:1
